title: Corpus Callosum Macrostructure and Microstructure in Relation to Interhemispheric Cortical Thickness Symmetry
content: Background: Although the corpus callosum is the principal commissure connecting the cerebral hemispheres, it remains unclear whether its macrostructure and microstructure are associated with greater structural symmetry between the hemispheres. Objective: To examine associations of callosal macrostructure and microstructure with left–right symmetry of cortical thickness in healthy developing children. Methods: In 8,131 children aged 9 to 10 from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (ABCD), we related 16 callosal measures to per-child hemispheric similarity indices computed across 75 paired cortical regions. Degree-of-symmetry indices are based on the mean absolute left-minus-right difference, reversed so that higher values denote greater symmetry; pattern indices express the correlation between the two hemispheric profiles. Results: All 16 callosal measures were positively associated with cortical thickness symmetry and 15 reached significance, the strongest at r = −.096. The probability that 16 measures would share a direction by chance is 3.1 × 10⁻⁵. Across 128 tests of callosal structure against hemispheric similarity, 51 reached significance against 6.4 expected. The yield was concentrated in magnitude indices rather than pattern indices. Conclusions: A larger and more myelinated corpus callosum accompanies hemispheres whose cortical thickness is more symmetrical. The association concerns the degree of symmetry rather than its regional pattern.
